danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 23
paragraphs: Fyrst Andrej havde brug for sin fars samtykke til ægteskabet og rejste næste dag til landet for at opnå det.

Hans far modtog sønnens meddelelse med udvendig fatning, men indvendig raseri. Han kunne ikke fatte, hvordan nogen kunne ønske at ændre sit liv eller indføre noget nyt i det, når hans eget liv allerede nærmede sig sin afslutning. »Bare de ville lade mig slutte mine dage, som jeg vil,« tænkte den gamle mand, »så kan de gøre, hvad de vil.« Over for sin søn anvendte han imidlertid den diplomati, han gemte til vigtige lejligheder, og idet han slog an i en rolig tone, drøftede han hele sagen.

For det første var ægteskabet ikke glimrende med hensyn til fødsel, rigdom eller rang. For det andet var fyrst Andrej ikke længere så ung, som han havde været, og hans helbred var dårligt (den gamle lagde særlig vægt på dette), mens hun var meget ung. For det tredje havde han en søn, som det ville være synd at betro til en uerfaren tøs. »For det fjerde og sidste,« sagde faderen og så ironisk på sin søn, »beder jeg dig om at udsætte det et år: rejs til udlandet, tag en kur, find den tyske huslærer til lille Nikolaj, som du ville. Hvis din kærlighed eller lidenskab eller stædighed — som du vil — stadig er lige stor derefter, så gift dig! Og det er mit sidste ord. Husk det, det sidste...« sluttede fyrsten i en tone, der viste, at intet ville få ham til at ændre sin beslutning.

Fyrst Andrej indså tydeligt, at den gamle mand håbede, at hans følelser, eller hans forlovedes, ikke ville holde et års prøve, eller at han (den gamle fyrste selv) ville dø inden da, og han besluttede at bøje sig for sin fars ønske — at fri og udsætte brylluppet et år.
Tre uger efter den sidste aften, han havde tilbragt hos familien Rostov, vendte fyrst Andrej tilbage til Petersborg.

Dagen efter sin samtale med sin mor ventede Natásha hele dagen på Bolkonskij, men han kom ikke. Den anden og den tredje dag var det det samme. Pierre kom heller ikke, og Natásha, der ikke vidste, at fyrst Andrej var rejst til sin far, kunne ikke forklare sig hans fravær.

Tre uger gik på den måde. Natásha havde ingen lyst til at gå nogen steder og vandrede fra værelse til værelse som en skygge, ørkesløs og sløv. Om natten græd hun i hemmelighed og gik ikke til sin mor om aftenen. Hun rødmede ustandseligt og var irritabel. Det forekom hende, at alle vidste om hendes skuffelse og lo af hende og ynkede hende. Hvor stærk end hendes indre sorg var, forstærkede dette sår på hendes forfængelighed hendes elendighed.
En dag kom hun til sin mor, forsøgte at sige noget og brast pludselig i gråd. Hendes tårer var som et fornærmet barns, der ikke ved, hvorfor det straffes.
Grevinden begyndte at trøste Natásha, som efter først at have lyttet til sin mors ord pludselig afbrød hende:
»Lad være, mama! Jeg tænker ikke, og jeg vil ikke tænke på det! Han kom bare, og så holdt han op, holdt op...«
Hendes stemme skælvede, og hun var atter nær ved at græde, men tog sig sammen og fortsatte stille:
»Og jeg ønsker slet ikke at gifte mig. Og jeg er bange for ham. Jeg er nu blevet helt rolig, helt rolig.«

Dagen efter denne samtale tog Natásha sin gamle kjole på, som hun vidste havde den særlige egenskab at fremkalde munterhed om morgenen, og vendte den dag tilbage til den gamle levemåde, hun havde opgivet siden ballet. Da hun havde drukket sin morgen-te, gik hun ud i balsalen, som hun særlig holdt af for dens stærke efterklang, og begyndte at synge sine solfeggioøvelser. Da hun var færdig med sin første øvelse, blev hun stående midt i rummet og sang en musikalsk frase, der særlig behagede hende. Hun lyttede glad (som om hun ikke havde ventet det) til charmen af tonerne, der genlød og fyldte hele den tomme balsal og langsomt døde bort. Og med ét følte hun sig glad. »Hvad nytter det at gøre så meget ud af det? Alting er godt, som det er,« sagde hun til sig selv, og hun begyndte at gå frem og tilbage i rummet, ikke simpelthen trædende på det klingende parketgulv, men med hvert skridt fra hæl til tå (hun havde et nyt og yndlingspar sko på) og lyttede lige så glad til det regelmæssige tik af hælen og knagen af tåen, som hun havde til sin egen stemmes lyd. Idet hun passerede et spejl, kastede hun et blik ind i det. »Se, det er mig!« syntes hendes ansigtsudtryk at sige, da hun fik øje på sig selv. »Ja, og rigtig pæn endda! Jeg behøver ingen.«

En tjener ville komme ind for at rydde noget op i rummet, men hun lod ham ikke, og efter at have lukket døren bag ham fortsatte hun sin vandring. Den morgen var hun vendt tilbage til sin yndlingsstemning — kærlighed til og glæde over sig selv. »Hvor er den Natásha dog charmerende!« sagde hun igen og talte som en tredje, kollektiv mandsperson. »Pæn, god stemme, ung og ikke i vejen for nogen, bare de lader hende i fred.« Men hvor meget de end lod hende i fred, kunne hun nu ikke være i fred og følte det straks.

I hallen åbnedes fordøren, og nogen spurgte: »Er herskabet hjemme?«, og derpå hørtes fodtrin. Natásha kiggede i spejlet, men så ikke sig selv. Hun lyttede til lydene i hallen. Da hun så sig selv, var hendes ansigt blegt. Det var ham. Det vidste hun med sikkerhed, skønt hun næppe hørte hans stemme gennem de lukkede døre.
Bleg og ophidset løb Natásha ind i dagligstuen.
»Mama! Bolkonskij er kommet!« sagde hun. »Mama, det er forfærdeligt, det er uudholdeligt! Jeg vil ikke... pines? Hvad skal jeg gøre?...«

Før grevinden kunne svare, trådte fyrst Andrej ind i rummet med et ophidset og alvorligt ansigt. Så snart han så Natásha, klarede hans ansigt op. Han kyssede grevindens hånd og Natáshas og satte sig ned ved sofaen.
»Det er længe siden, vi har haft den fornøjelse...« begyndte grevinden, men fyrst Andrej afbrød hende ved at svare på hendes påtænkte spørgsmål, tydeligvis i hast for at sige, hvad han måtte sige.

»Jeg har ikke besøgt Dem hele denne tid, fordi jeg har været hos min far. Jeg var nødt til at drøfte en meget vigtig sag med ham. Jeg kom først hjem i aftes,« sagde han med et blik på Natásha. »Jeg ønsker at tale med Dem, grevinde,« tilføjede han efter et øjebliks pause.
Grevinden sænkede øjnene med et dybt suk.
»Jeg står til Deres tjeneste,« mumlede hun.
Natásha vidste, at hun burde gå, men var ude af stand til det; noget greb hende om halsen, og uden hensyn til manerer stirrede hun med vidt opspærrede øjne lige på fyrst Andrej.
»Med det samme? I dette øjeblik!... Nej, det kan ikke være!« tænkte hun.
Igen så han på hende, og dette blik overbeviste hende om, at hun ikke tog fejl. Ja, straks, i dette øjeblik, ville hendes skæbne blive afgjort.
»Gå, Natásha! Jeg kalder på dig,« sagde grevinden hviskende.
Natásha kiggede med forskræmte, bønfaldende øjne på fyrst Andrej og sin mor og gik ud.
»Jeg er kommet, grevinde, for at bede om Deres datters hånd,« sagde fyrst Andrej.
Grevindens ansigt blussede op, men hun sagde intet.

»Deres tilbud...« begyndte hun omsider roligt. Han forblev tavs og så hende i øjnene. »Deres tilbud...« (hun blev forvirret) »er os kært, og jeg accepterer Deres tilbud. Jeg er glad. Og min mand... jeg håber... men det vil afhænge af hende...«
»Jeg taler med hende, når jeg har Deres samtykke... Giver De mig det?« sagde fyrst Andrej.

»Ja,« svarede grevinden. Hun rakte ham sin hånd og trykkede med en blanding af fremmedfølelse og ømhed sine læber mod hans pande, da han bøjede sig for at kysse hendes hånd. Hun ønskede at elske ham som en søn, men følte, at han for hende var en fremmed og skræmmende mand. »Jeg er sikker på, at min mand vil samtykke,« sagde grevinden, »men Deres far...«

»Min far, hvem jeg har meddelt mine planer, har sat det som en udtrykkelig betingelse for sit samtykke, at brylluppet ikke må finde sted før om et år. Og det ønskede jeg at fortælle Dem,« sagde fyrst Andrej.
»Det er sandt, at Natásha stadig er ung, men — så længe?...«
»Det kan ikke undgås,« sagde fyrst Andrej med et suk.
»Jeg sender hende ind til Dem,« sagde grevinden og forlod rummet.
»Herre, forbarm Dig over os!« gentog hun, mens hun ledte efter sin datter.

Sonja sagde, at Natásha var på sit soveværelse. Natásha sad på sengen, bleg og med tørre øjne, og stirrede på ikonerne, mens hun hviskede noget og hurtigt korsede sig. Da hun så sin mor, sprang hun op og fløj hen til hende.
»Nå, mama?... Nå?...«
»Gå ind til ham. Han beder om din hånd,« sagde grevinden, køligt syntes Natásha. »Gå... gå,« sagde moderen trist og bebrejdende med et dybt suk, mens hendes datter løb af sted.

Natásha huskede aldrig, hvordan hun kom ind i dagligstuen. Da hun kom ind og så ham, standsede hun. »Er det muligt, at denne fremmede nu er blevet alt for mig?« spurgte hun sig selv og svarede straks: »Ja, alt! Han alene er mig nu kærere end alt i verden.« Fyrst Andrej kom hen til hende med sænkede øjne.
»Jeg har elsket dig fra det allerførste øjeblik, jeg så dig. Tør jeg håbe?«

Han så på hende og blev slået af det alvorlige, lidenskabelige udtryk i hendes ansigt. Hendes ansigt sagde: »Hvorfor spørge? Hvorfor tvivle på, hvad du ikke kan undgå at vide? Hvorfor tale, når ord ikke kan udtrykke, hvad man føler?«
Hun nærmede sig ham og standsede. Han tog hendes hånd og kyssede den.
»Elsker du mig?«
»Ja, ja!« mumlede Natásha som i fortrydelse. Så sukkede hun dybt, og idet hun trak vejret hurtigere og hurtigere, begyndte hun at hulke.
»Hvad er der? Hvad er der i vejen?«
»Åh, jeg er så lykkelig!« svarede hun, smilede gennem sine tårer, bøjede sig nærmere mod ham, tøvede et øjeblik, som om hun spurgte sig selv, om hun måtte, og kyssede ham derpå.

Fyrst Andrej holdt hendes hænder, så ind i hendes øjne og fandt ikke i sit hjerte sin tidligere kærlighed til hende. Noget i ham var pludselig forandret; der var ikke længere den tidligere poetiske og mystiske charme af begær, men der var medlidenhed med hendes kvindelige og barnlige svaghed, frygt for hendes hengivenhed og tillid, og en trykkende, men dog glædelig følelse af den pligt, der nu bandt ham til hende for evigt. Den nuværende følelse, skønt ikke så lys og poetisk som den tidligere, var stærkere og mere alvorlig.
»Har din mor fortalt dig, at det ikke kan ske før om et år?« spurgte fyrst Andrej, stadig seende ind i hendes øjne.

»Er det muligt, at jeg — den 'lille tøs', som alle kaldte mig,« tænkte Natásha, »er det muligt, at jeg nu skal være dette fremmede, kære, kloge menneskes hustru og ligemand, som selv min far ser op til? Kan det være sandt? Kan det være sandt, at man nu ikke mere kan lege med livet, at jeg nu er voksen, at der nu hviler et ansvar på mig for hvert eneste ord og hver eneste handling? Ja, men hvad var det, han spurgte mig om?«
»Nej,« svarede hun, men hun havde ikke forstået hans spørgsmål.
»Tilgiv mig!« sagde han. »Men du er så ung, og jeg har allerede gennemlevet så meget. Jeg er bange for dig — du kender endnu ikke dig selv.«
Natásha lyttede med anspændt opmærksomhed og forsøgte, men uden held, at fatte meningen af hans ord.

»Hvor hårdt end dette år, der forsinker min lykke, bliver,« fortsatte fyrst Andrej, »vil det give dig tid til at blive sikker på dig selv. Jeg beder dig om at gøre mig lykkelig om et år, men du er fri: vores forlovelse skal forblive en hemmelighed, og hvis du finder ud af, at du ikke elsker mig, eller hvis du kommer til at elske...« sagde fyrst Andrej med et unaturligt smil.
»Hvorfor siger du det?« afbrød Natásha ham. »Du ved, at lige fra den dag, du først kom til Otrádnoe, har jeg elsket dig,« råbte hun, fuldt overbevist om, at hun talte sandt.
»Om et år vil du lære dig selv at kende...«
»Et helt år!« gentog Natásha pludselig, først nu indseende at brylluppet skulle udsættes et år. »Men hvorfor et år? Hvorfor et år?...«
Fyrst Andrej begyndte at forklare hende grundene til denne udsættelse. Natásha hørte ham ikke.
»Og kan det ikke hjælpes?« spurgte hun. Fyrst Andrej svarede ikke, men hans ansigt udtrykte det umulige i at ændre den beslutning.

»Det er forfærdeligt! Åh, det er forfærdeligt! Forfærdeligt!« udbrød Natásha pludselig og brast igen i gråd. »Jeg dør af at vente et år — det er umuligt, det er forfærdeligt!« Hun så ind i sin elskedes ansigt og så deri et udtryk af medlidenhed og rådvildhed.
»Nej, nej! Jeg gør alt!« sagde hun og standsede pludselig sine tårer. »Jeg er så lykkelig.«
Faderen og moderen kom ind i stuen og gav det forlovede par deres velsignelse.
Fra den dag begyndte fyrst Andrej at komme jævnligt hos familien Rostov som Natáshas forlovede.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 23
paragraphs: Prince Andrew needed his father's consent to the marriage, and the next day he set off for the country to obtain it.

His father received his son's news with outward calm but inner fury. He could not understand how anyone could wish to change his life or introduce anything new when his own life was already nearing its end. "If only they would let me finish my days in peace," the old man thought, "then they can do as they please." With his son, however, he employed the diplomacy he reserved for important occasions and, adopting a calm tone, discussed the whole matter.

First of all, the marriage was not a brilliant one as regards birth, wealth, or rank. Second, Prince Andrew was no longer young, and his health was poor — the old man stressed this particularly — while she was very young. Third, he had a son whom it would be a pity to entrust to a slip of a girl. "Fourth and finally," the father said, looking at his son with irony, "I ask you to put it off for a year. Go abroad, take a cure, find a German tutor for little Nicholas as you planned. Then if your love or passion or stubbornness — call it what you will — is still as strong, marry! And that's my last word on it. Remember — the last..." the prince concluded, in a tone that made clear nothing would change his mind.

Prince Andrew could see clearly that the old man hoped either his feelings or his fiancee's would not survive a year's test, or that he himself would die before then. He decided to comply with his father's wish — to propose and postpone the wedding for a year.
Three weeks after his last evening with the Rostovs, Prince Andrew returned to Petersburg.

The day after her conversation with her mother, Natasha waited for Bolkonsky all day, but he didn't come. It was the same on the second and third days. Pierre didn't come either, and Natasha, not knowing that Prince Andrew had gone to see his father, could not explain his absence.

Three weeks went by like this. Natasha had no desire to go out anywhere and drifted from room to room like a shadow, idle and listless; she cried in secret at night and no longer came to her mother in the evenings. She blushed constantly and was irritable. It seemed to her that everyone knew about her disappointment and was laughing at her and pitying her. As strong as her inner grief was, this wound to her vanity only made her misery worse.
Once she came to her mother, tried to say something, and suddenly burst into tears. Her tears were those of an offended child who doesn't understand why it's being punished.
The countess began to comfort Natasha, who at first listened to her mother's words but then suddenly cut her off:
"Stop it, Mama! I don't think about it and I don't want to think about it! He just came and then stopped, stopped..."
Her voice trembled and she nearly cried again, but she recovered and went on quietly:
"And I don't want to get married at all. And I'm afraid of him; I've become quite calm now, quite calm."

The day after this conversation Natasha put on an old dress that she knew had the special property of making her feel cheerful in the morning, and that day she returned to the old way of life she had abandoned since the ball. After morning tea she went to the ballroom, which she particularly loved for its resonant acoustics, and began singing her vocal exercises. When she finished her first exercise she stopped in the middle of the room and sang a musical phrase that especially pleased her. She listened joyfully — as though she hadn't expected it — to the charm of the notes reverberating, filling the whole empty ballroom, and slowly dying away; and all at once she felt cheerful. "What's the point of making such a fuss about it? Things are perfectly fine as they are," she told herself, and she began pacing the room — not simply walking on the resonant parquet but stepping with each step from heel to toe, in a new and favorite pair of shoes, and listening to the rhythmic tap of the heel and creak of the toe with as much pleasure as she had listened to her own singing. Passing a mirror she glanced into it. "There — that's me!" her expression seemed to say. "Well, and very nice too! I don't need anybody."

A footman tried to come in to clear something from the room, but she wouldn't let him. Having shut the door behind him, she continued her walk. That morning she had returned to her favorite mood — love of and delight in herself. "What a charming girl that Natasha is!" she said again, speaking as if she were some third, collective, male person. "Pretty, a good voice, young, and not in anyone's way if only they'd leave her alone." But however much she was left alone, she couldn't be at peace now, and she immediately sensed this.

In the hall the front door opened, and someone asked "Is the family at home?" and then there were footsteps. Natasha was looking in the mirror but didn't see herself. She was listening to the sounds in the hall. When she caught sight of her own face, it was pale. It was him. She was certain of it, though she could barely hear his voice through the closed doors.
Pale and agitated, Natasha ran into the drawing room.
"Mama! Bolkonsky is here!" she said. "Mama, this is terrible, it's unbearable! I don't want... to be tormented! What am I supposed to do?..."

Before the countess could answer, Prince Andrew entered the room with an agitated, serious face. The moment he saw Natasha his face brightened. He kissed the countess's hand and Natasha's and sat down beside the sofa.
"It's been so long since we had the pleasure..." the countess began, but Prince Andrew interrupted her by answering her intended question, clearly in a hurry to say what he had come to say.

"I haven't been to see you all this time because I was at my father's. I needed to discuss a very important matter with him. I only got back last night," he said, glancing at Natasha. "I need to speak with you, Countess," he added after a moment's pause.
The countess lowered her eyes, sighing deeply.
"I am at your disposal," she murmured.
Natasha knew she ought to leave, but couldn't. Something gripped her throat, and ignoring all propriety she stared straight at Prince Andrew with wide-open eyes.
"Now? This very instant?... No, it can't be!" she thought.
He glanced at her again, and that glance convinced her she was not mistaken. Yes — right now, this very instant, her fate would be decided.
"Go, Natasha! I'll call you," said the countess in a whisper.
Natasha looked at Prince Andrew and at her mother with frightened, imploring eyes and went out.
"I have come, Countess, to ask for your daughter's hand," said Prince Andrew.
The countess's face flushed hotly, but she said nothing.

"Your offer..." she began at last, speaking with an effort at composure. He remained silent, looking into her eyes. "Your offer..." she grew confused, "is welcome to us, and I accept your offer. I am glad. And my husband... I hope... but it will depend on her..."
"I will speak to her when I have your consent... Do you give it to me?" said Prince Andrew.

"Yes," replied the countess. She held out her hand to him, and with a mingled feeling of strangeness and tenderness pressed her lips to his forehead as he stooped to kiss her hand. She wanted to love him as a son but felt he was a stranger, a daunting man. "I'm sure my husband will agree," said the countess, "but your father..."
"My father, to whom I have told my plans, has made it an express condition that the wedding not take place for a year. And I wanted to tell you of that," said Prince Andrew.
"It's true that Natasha is still young, but — that long?..."
"It can't be helped," said Prince Andrew with a sigh.
"I will send her to you," said the countess, and left the room.
"Lord have mercy on us!" she repeated as she went to find her daughter.

Sonya said Natasha was in her bedroom. Natasha was sitting on the bed, pale and dry-eyed, staring at the icons and whispering something as she rapidly crossed herself. Seeing her mother she jumped up and flew to her.
"Well, Mama?... Well?..."
"Go, go to him. He is asking for your hand," said the countess, coldly it seemed to Natasha. "Go... go," said the mother, sadly and reproachfully, with a deep sigh, as her daughter rushed away.

Natasha never remembered how she entered the drawing room. When she walked in and saw him, she stopped. "Is it possible that this stranger has now become everything to me?" she asked herself, and immediately answered: "Yes, everything! He alone is now dearer to me than everything in the world." Prince Andrew came toward her with lowered eyes.
"I have loved you from the very first moment I saw you. May I hope?"
He looked at her and was struck by the serious, passionate expression on her face. Her face said: "Why ask? Why doubt what you cannot help but know? Why put into words what words can never express?"
She moved closer to him and stopped. He took her hand and kissed it.
"Do you love me?"
"Yes, yes!" Natasha whispered, almost crossly. Then she sighed deeply and, catching her breath faster and faster, began to sob.
"What is it? What's the matter?"
"Oh, I'm so happy!" she answered, smiled through her tears, leaned closer to him, paused for a moment as if asking herself whether she might, and then kissed him.

Prince Andrew held her hands, looked into her eyes, and did not find in his heart his former love for her. Something in him had suddenly changed; there was no longer the old poetic and mystical pull of desire, but instead pity for her feminine and childish vulnerability, awe at her devotion and trust, and a heavy yet joyful sense of the duty that now bound him to her forever. The present feeling, though not as bright and poetic as the earlier one, was stronger and more serious.
"Did your mother tell you it cannot be for a year?" asked Prince Andrew, still looking into her eyes.

"Is it possible that I — the 'little girl,' as everyone called me," thought Natasha, "is it possible that I am now to be the wife and equal of this strange, dear, clever man whom even my father looks up to? Can it be true? Can it be true that there can be no more playing at life, that now I am grown up, that I am responsible for my every word and deed? Yes, but what did he just ask me?"
"No," she replied, but she hadn't understood his question.
"Forgive me," he said. "But you are so young, and I have already been through so much. I am afraid for you — you don't yet know yourself."
Natasha listened with intense concentration, trying but failing to grasp the meaning of his words.

"Difficult as this year of delay will be — the year that postpones my happiness," continued Prince Andrew, "it will give you time to be sure of yourself. I ask you to make me happy in a year, but you are free: our engagement shall remain a secret, and should you find that you don't love me, or should you come to love..." said Prince Andrew with a forced smile.
"Why do you say that?" Natasha interrupted. "You know that from the very day you first came to Otradnoe I have loved you," she cried, completely convinced she was speaking the truth.
"In a year you will learn to know yourself..."
"A whole year!" Natasha repeated suddenly, only now grasping that the wedding was to be postponed for a year. "But why a year? Why a year?..."
Prince Andrew began to explain the reasons for the delay. Natasha didn't hear him.
"And there's no way around it?" she asked. Prince Andrew did not answer, but his face made clear that the decision could not be changed.

"It's awful! Oh, it's awful! Awful!" Natasha suddenly cried, and burst into sobs again. "I'll die waiting a year — it's impossible, it's awful!" She looked into her lover's face and saw in it an expression of sympathy and bewilderment.
"No, no! I'll do anything!" she said, suddenly stopping her tears. "I'm so happy."
The father and mother came into the room and gave the engaged couple their blessing.
From that day Prince Andrew began coming to the Rostovs' as Natasha's fiance.
